preamble: Depalatalization of [pʲ] to plain [p] removes the palatal secondary articulation of a labial stop. Palatalized labials are perceptually weak in coda position, where the palatal release has no following vowel to carry it, and several Slavic languages hardened word-final soft labials. In Polish the change took place in Middle Polish and the old softness survives only before vowel-initial endings (karp, gen. karpia 'carp'); Ukrainian likewise has no palatalized labials word-finally (степ vs Russian степь 'steppe').

examples.from: Middle Polish karp' [karpʲ] 'carp' (soft stem; cf. gen. karpia [ˈkarpʲa])
examples.note: Labials were depalatalized in coda position in Middle Polish; the soft stem is preserved in the oblique cases (karpia, karpie), just as in gołąb, gen. gołębia 'pigeon'.
Ukrainian lost palatalization in word-final labials (compare Russian степь [sʲtʲepʲ], which keeps it).

sources: Czaplicki, B. (2010). Palatalized Labials in Polish Dialects: An Evolutionary Perspective. Journal of Slavic Linguistics 18(2), 259–290. https://ojs.ung.si/index.php/JSL/article/view/134
Shevelov, G. Y. (1979). A Historical Phonology of the Ukrainian Language. Carl Winter. https://lccn.loc.gov/80494566
